AbstractData-intensive collider experiments increasingly require models that transfer across high-dimensional, partially observed measurements, yet most analyses still optimize separate models for each task. Here, to address this bottleneck, we introduce EVENET, an event-level foundation model pretrained on 500 million simulated collision events using self-supervised learning and physics-informed supervision. The model constructs a shared particle-cloud representation from the variable-length set of physics objects in each event. Across searches for heavy resonances and exotic Higgs decays, EVENET outperforms both established and state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in low-statistics regimes. We validate transfer to experimental data by rediscovering the ϒ meson in CMS Open Data. The pretrained model also supports precise extraction of quantum-correlation observables that remain stable under the tested systematic variations. Together, these results establish a reusable backbone for diverse collider analyses, improving downstream adaptation after a substantial one-time pretraining investment.

Phenomenology

High-Energy Particle Collision Data Analysis

MainFoundation models have reshaped how large-scale data are analysed across science and engineering. In natural language processing, self-supervised pretraining on massive text corpora produces general-purpose representations that transfer efficiently to diverse downstream tasks with minimal fine-tuning, as demonstrated by BERT1 and GPT2. In computer vision, contrastive learning and masked autoencoders3,4 have matched or exceeded fully supervised baselines by learning from unlabelled images alone. More recently, this pretrain-then-transfer paradigm has permeated the natural sciences: protein language models predict atomic-level structures from amino acid sequences5, and self-supervised encoders extract robust imaging biomarkers from limited clinical cohorts6. A common lesson from these domains is that large-scale pretraining on domain data captures latent structure that generalizes far more efficiently than task-specific training, particularly when labelled data are scarce7.High-energy physics faces a data landscape similar to that of other fields. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC)8 delivers billions of proton–proton collisions per year, each recorded as a variable-length set of final-state particles whose properties encode the physics of the underlying hard scattering. Extracting insight from these high-dimensional, partially observed records is central to the LHC programme, spanning searches for new resonances, measurements of rare decay channels and precision tests of the standard model (SM). Machine learning has become essential for jet tagging9,10, event classification11, anomaly detection12,13 and fast simulation14, consistently surpassing traditional multivariate approaches15. Yet the prevailing paradigm remains one of task-specific optimization: for each new analysis, a dedicated model is designed, trained on purpose-built labelled simulations and validated independently. This imposes increasing costs in expert effort, computing resources and turnaround time that will intensify as the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC)16 increases both data volumes and the demand for sensitivity to rare processes. The same challenge also constrains current particle physics experiments, such as Belle II17, DUNE18 and future collider experiments.Initial steps towards foundation models in collider physics have focused on individual jets, learning substructure representations for tagging and classification19,20,21. Weakly supervised and self-supervised methods have also been explored for model-agnostic anomaly detection22,23,24,25,26,27. Although promising, these efforts remain limited in scope. Most operate on single physics objects rather than full collision events. Existing approaches for full events are typically limited to a few downstream tasks28 or narrow physics process coverage29, leaving open whether the learned representations transfer across diverse collider analyses. Furthermore, the critical step of validating learned representations on real experimental data, as opposed to simulation alone, has received little attention30.Here we introduce EVENET, an event-level foundation model for particle collision data that addresses these limitations (Fig. 1). EVENET represents each collision as an unordered particle cloud and processes it using a shared point–edge transformer backbone. Interchangeable task heads support process classification, object-to-resonance assignment, final-state segmentation, and diffusion-based reconstruction of masked or undetected particles. The backbone is pretrained on 500 million simulated events through a two-stage strategy combining self-supervised learning (SSL) with physics-informed supervision. We evaluate its generalization, simulation-to-data transfer, data efficiency, systematic robustness across new-physics searches, resonance rediscovery in open data from the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment, and precision quantum-correlation measurements. The resulting backbone is designed for repeated downstream adaptation after a substantial one-time pretraining investment.Fig. 1: Overview of the EVENET model architecture and tasks.Full size imagea, Collision events are reconstructed as sets of physics objects, which form the input to a point–edge transformer encoder. Task-specific decoders extend this shared representation to both generative and discriminative objectives. b, Self-supervised generation (SS-Gen) reconstructs masked input objects (or generates complete events), whereas supervised generation (Sup-Gen) predicts target particles conditioned on observed objects using diffusion. c, Discriminative decoders branch into three task heads aligned with common analysis goals: identifying the physics process (Cls), matching reconstructed objects to their parent resonances (Asn) and grouping objects into final-state categories for event interpretation (Seg). MLP, multilayer perceptron.ResultsWe evaluate EVENET, an end-to-end event-level foundation model designed to learn a unified representation across a heterogeneous set of analysis tasks. EVENET operates directly on variable-length particle-cloud inputs using a single backbone that can be applied across diverse observational regimes, including fully reconstructed, partially reconstructed and noise-perturbed events.The backbone is pretrained with approximately balanced event counts across the process–final-state channels listed in Extended Data Table 1, without cross-section-based event weighting or sampling, thereby avoiding the underrepresentation of rare processes. Pretraining follows the hybrid pretraining strategy described in ‘Pretraining strategy selection’: (1) a self-supervised masking phase, followed by (2) a joint optimization phase combining self-supervised and supervised objectives. We then benchmark a suite of downstream tasks that separately probe generalization (‘Generalization across hypothesis grids for discovery’), simulation-to-data transfer (‘Simulation-to-data transfer with resonance rediscovery’), multi-task reconstruction and robustness to detector-level systematic variations (‘Physics-structured multi-task synergy and robustness’) and training efficiency (‘Training convergence’).Pretraining strategy selectionTo quantify the contribution of the proposed pretraining strategy, we compare three EVENET variants that differ only in their pretraining objectives while sharing an identical backbone architecture and downstream fine-tuning procedure.Table 1 summarizes the prediction heads used during each pretraining stage and downstream application, and implementation details are provided in ‘Training procedure, software and hardware’ in Methods. These correspond to the task-specific decoder heads shown in Fig. 1. During stage I, only the self-supervised generative head (SS-Gen) is optimized through masked-particle reconstruction, encouraging the backbone to learn task-agnostic event representations. Stage II adds the supervised generation (Sup-Gen) and classification (Cls) objectives to further refine the shared representation. The assignment (Asn) and segmentation (Seg) heads are task-specific and are therefore trained only during downstream fine-tuning.Table 1 Pretraining and downstream training configurationsFull size tableWe isolate the contribution of each stage through the following three model variants:

EVENET–Scratch (Scratch) is trained from random initialization on each downstream task and serves as the no-pretraining baseline.

EVENET–SSL (SSL) is initialized from the stage I pretrained checkpoint and therefore isolates the benefit of task-agnostic representation learning before introducing physics-informed supervision.

EVENET–Full (Full) is initialized from the complete two-stage pretrained model before downstream fine-tuning.

These variants correspond to no pretraining, stage I only and the complete two-stage strategy, respectively. Together, they provide the primary controlled comparison of successive pretraining stages within a common architecture. A complementary classification-only control, described in Supplementary Information, tests conventional supervised transfer using the same backbone and pretraining corpus.Generalization across hypothesis grids for discoverySearches for new physics often require exploring large parameter spaces with many signal hypotheses, each supported by limited simulated data. Models must therefore remain reliable across a wide range of kinematic conditions.We illustrate this challenge with searches for a heavy new particle decaying into a lighter new particle and a SM Higgs boson (X → YHSM), as motivated by several beyond-SM scenarios31,32,33. We evaluate this benchmark using fully simulated CMS Open Data. Because the pretraining samples (‘Monte Carlo simulation and Open Data’ in Methods) contain no pile-up (multiple interactions within the same bunch crossing), this benchmark tests robustness to domain shifts arising from pile-up and differences in detector response.We consider cases where the lighter particle decays into two bottom quarks and the Higgs boson decays into a pair of W bosons (\(b{\overline{b}}{WW}^{* }\)), where one W decays to a charged lepton and a neutrino (ℓν) and the other decays to two quarks (qq). Although the pretraining dataset includes SM HSM → WW* events, which constitute approximately 12.8% of the retained pretraining corpus, it contains no X → YHSM topology. Together, this unseen production topology and the distinctive \(b{\overline{b}}{WW}^{* }\) final state provide a demanding test of whether learned global event representations transfer beyond the pretraining distribution.We compare EVENET, fine-tuned through its classification head (Fig. 1), with two tabular baselines: XGBoost34, an established method in high-energy physics, and TabPFN35,36, a pretrained foundation model for tabular classification. Both operate on fixed-length tables of human-engineered event features, whereas EVENET processes variable-length point clouds of reconstructed objects. For each method, a separate classifier is trained at each point in the (mX, mY) mass grid. (5) Ratio of the maximum SIC obtained with each baseline method to that obtained with the pretrained EVENET–Full model.Simulation-to-data transfer with resonance rediscoveryQuarkonium fragmentation within jets provides an important test of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) by probing the transition between perturbative and non-perturbative scales38,39,40,41. While charmonium production inside jets has been extensively studied42,43, bottomonium in the anti-isolated regime, where the decay muons are embedded in substantial surrounding hadronic activity, remains largely unexplored. This phase space is difficult to access with standard isolation-based dimuon selections, while relaxing the isolation requirement introduces a large combinatorial background that obscures the ϒ signal. These features make anti-isolated ϒ production a challenging anomaly-detection benchmark44. We therefore search for anti-isolated ϒ → μ+μ− decays in the 2016 CMS Open Data dimuon dataset45. As the analysis is fully data-driven, it provides a direct test of whether the simulation-pretrained EVENET representation transfers to collision data.Following the CATHODE strategy44,46, we learn a background model from the dimuon-mass sidebands, interpolate it into the signal region and search for discrepancies with the data. Whereas ref. 44 models low-dimensional engineered observables using a conditional normalizing flow, the diffusion-based EVENET self-supervised generative head models low-level particle-cloud kinematic and vertex information. The generated clouds are calibrated to restore the conditioned dimuon mass and momentum balance, with the required correction providing a diagnostic of generation fidelity.We then train an XGBoost classifier, following ref. 44, to distinguish the observed signal-region data from the generated background using observables derived from the particle clouds. The classifier is designed to be mass independent to avoid artificially sculpting a resonance. Its output score, \(z({\bf{x}})=\frac{{p}_{\mathrm{data}}({\bf{x}})}{{p}_{\mathrm{data}}({\bf{x}})+{p}_{\mathrm{bkg}}({\bf{x}})},\) is converted into an estimate of the signal-to-background likelihood ratio$$\ell ({\bf{x}})\equiv \frac{z({\bf{x}})-(1-\mu )(1-z({\bf{x}}))}{\mu (1-z({\bf{x}}))}=\frac{{p}_{\mathrm{signal}}({\bf{x}})}{{p}_{\mathrm{bkg}}({\bf{x}})}.$$

This quantity serves as the most powerful mass-independent test statistic47,48. Events are weighted by ℓ(x), and the local significance is extracted from the reweighted dimuon-mass spectrum. Each pseudo-experiment resamples the generated background and retrains the classifier with independent randomization; performance is quantified by the median significance and its spread across pseudo-experiments. The contrast between the pretrained and scratch models therefore highlights the importance of pretraining in mitigating this challenge.Physics-structured multi-task synergy and robustnessTo test whether a single pretrained event representation can support structurally different collider analyses, we consider two multi-head downstream tasks: an out-of-distribution exotic Higgs search and a high-statistics precision quantum-correlation measurement in dileptonic top-quark pair events. In both cases, performance depends on jointly optimizing heads that address complementary aspects of event reconstruction, allowing us to test whether pretraining supports multiple structured objectives. Because detector-response mismodelling can bias inference, we also assess robustness by applying representative detector-level variations at evaluation time without retraining, isolating representation stability under detector-induced distribution shifts from re-optimization effects. In this section, training sizes are reported relative to task-specific reference datasets: 200,000 events for the exotic Higgs search and 1 million events for the quantum-correlation measurement. These reference sizes reflect typical LHC analysis statistics. All methods use validation-based early stopping and comparisons use each model’s best-performing checkpoint.Exotic Higgs searchDirect searches for exotic Higgs decays remain a central probe of physics beyond the SM, with strong motivation for rare non-standard final states49,50. We report the maximum SIC, corresponding to the classifier threshold that maximizes it. These correlations define entanglement-sensitive observables and have been recently measured by ATLAS and CMS58,59.Full event reconstruction remains the dominant limitation because the two neutrinos and finite detector resolution leave the kinematic system under-constrained. Measurement precision therefore depends critically on neutrino momentum inference and object assignment. We address this using physics-structured particle-assignment and supervised generative heads that jointly resolve combinatorial ambiguities and infer the missing neutrino momenta.Spin-correlation coefficients Cij are reconstructed using the decay-angle formalism described in Methods (equations (8) and (9)), and combined into the entanglement-sensitive observable Δ = ∣Ckk + Crr∣ − Cnn − 1, for which Δ > 0 indicates quantum entanglement56. Measurement performance is quantified using the precision metric σΔ/Δ. All evaluated configurations yield Δ > 0, ensuring that the precision is well defined. This comparison excludes the one-time pretraining cost reported ‘Training procedure, software and hardware’ in Methods.DiscussionIn this study, we introduce EVENET, a foundation model for high-energy physics analysis. Across four downstream settings spanning precision measurement, new-physics searches and collision-data anomaly detection, EVENET–Full attains performance comparable to or better than task-specific state-of-the-art baselines and the pretrained tabular foundation model TabPFN. Within the common architecture, this two-stage pretraining model also matches or outperforms the variants with no pretraining (EVENET–Scratch) or one-stage pretraining (EVENET–SSL), often requiring substantially fewer optimization steps during fine-tuning (Fig. 2 and ‘Training convergence’). Unlike previous particle-based pretraining approaches focused on discriminative tasks28,29, EVENET uses hybrid discriminative-generative pretraining to learn a shared particle-cloud representation supporting both inference-driven analyses and generative reconstruction across diverse physics processes and data domains. This hybrid pretraining strategy also highlights a central lesson of this work: whereas SSL alone is often sufficient in other domains, pretraining on collider data with explicit physical structure can exploit unambiguous simulation truth labels as strong inductive signals. In our experiments, incorporating this supervision improves upon SSL-only pretraining.Across disparate downstream regimes, a shared pattern emerges: a single pretrained backbone can be adapted efficiently across heterogeneous inference settings without loss of physics performance. In searches for heavy Higgs bosons, EVENET uses a shared pretrained initialization across scan points, enabling efficient per-hypothesis fine-tuning and avoiding the need to train models from scratch at each mass hypothesis, while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art and tabular foundation-model baselines across strongly varying kinematics. This advantage is reflected in the training dynamics: pretrained variants reach lower validation loss with substantially fewer optimization steps during downstream adaptation. The substantial one-time pretraining cost can be amortized through reuse of the backbone across multiple analyses.A complementary effect appears when downstream objectives depend explicitly on event topology or multi-step inference. In exotic Higgs decays, models trained from scratch benefit from auxiliary assignment or segmentation heads, reflecting the discriminative value of resonance structure. For EVENET–Full, however, this auxiliary gain is reduced: high sensitivity is already achieved using the classification head alone. These observations suggest that, with pretraining, human-designed auxiliary heads become less essential, lowering reliance on task-specific architectural augmentation during fine-tuning. Moreover, stable end-to-end training is maintained even when the downstream loss couples multiple inference targets. We observe this robustness not only in the new-physics search setting above but also in quantum-correlation measurements, which require the joint inference of resonance assignment and neutrino reconstruction, and in which measurement uncertainties are often driven by systematic effects rather than statistical fluctuations. Taken together, these aspects highlight the potential of the pretrained backbone to tackle complex, analysis-grade problems.This cross-task coherence extends to self-supervised generative deployment on collision data. In anomaly detection, EVENET–Full maintains stable performance across detector and kinematic regimes, including low-statistics settings, surpassing the published benchmark after calibrated reconstruction (median significance \(7.{6}_{-0.4}^{+0.4}\sigma\) versus 6.4σ in ref. 44). Models trained from scratch instead show a lower post-calibration significance and require substantially larger kinematic corrections.Together, these results support the use of a unified event-level foundation model as a practical substrate for both discriminative and generative analyses, consolidating traditionally multi-stage pipelines into a single backbone while retaining robustness to the systematic variations evaluated here.Despite these advances, several challenges remain. Although EVENET incorporates noise-tolerance training, it is not yet a fully uncertainty-aware framework: explicit modelling and propagation of detector systematics and theoretical uncertainties remain necessary for rigorous statistical interpretation. In addition, while multi-head architectures are effective in practice, predictions from different heads are not explicitly constrained to be mutually consistent, leaving scope for future approaches that jointly enforce coherence across classification, assignment and generative reconstruction outputs. Transfer to collision data is encouraging, but systematic stress tests under substantial simulation-data mismodelling have not yet been performed. Finally, although the shared particle-cloud representation captures event structure and kinematics, a detailed analysis of latent-space organization and interpretability is deferred to future work.In conclusion, EVENET illustrates the promise of event-level foundation models as a flexible framework for a broad class of analyses. Deployment in LHC analyses will provide a decisive test of its ability to streamline end-to-end inference, particularly when integrated with object-level frameworks such as OmniLearned27. Looking ahead, coupling EVENET to differentiable detectors14 or fast-simulation frameworks61 could enable more tightly integrated analysis pipelines, supporting gradient-based optimization from reconstructed observables towards theory parameters. At the same time, the learned shared particle-cloud representation suggests opportunities for more interpretable embeddings and anomaly-sensitive representations. Taken together, these results position EVENET as a concrete step towards foundation models for collider physics, with a clear near-term validation milestone and a restrained longer-term outlook.MethodsIn this section, we give implementation-level details on dataset preparation, model architecture and training set-up. We also clarify how the downstream analyses were carried out and formalize the performance metrics used in our studies.Monte Carlo simulation and Open DataTo generate datasets for both pretraining and downstream studies, we used large-scale Monte Carlo simulations covering a broad spectrum of SM processes. SM hard-scattering processes are generated with MADGRAPH5_aMC@NLO 3.5.562, covering multijet backgrounds, top-quark final states and electroweak boson final states across a range of jet multiplicities. Parton showering and hadronization are modelled with PYTHIA 863, and detector responses are approximated using Delphes64 with a generic detector configuration. All samples produced with this Delphes chain correspond to proton–proton collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of \(\sqrt{s}=13\,\mathrm{TeV}\) and are generated without pile-up.Generator-level preselections define the phase-space support of the event representation and suppress low-energy or out-of-acceptance configurations. Reconstructed jets and charged leptons are required to satisfy a transverse momentum pT > 10 GeV, with charged leptons restricted by imposing a pseudorapidity requirement of ∣η∣ < 2.5, where η represents the angle of a particle relative to the beam pipe. Additional process-dependent filters enforce minimal object multiplicities consistent with the underlying hard process; for example, QCD samples require at least two jets with pT > 20 GeV, while top-quark and electroweak samples impose lepton, jet and b-jet multiplicity requirements matching the target final states.The pretraining corpus comprises approximately 3 × 109 simulated SM events, from which about 5 × 108 events are retained after preselections. These samples span the dominant LHC background and signal-like processes and are used exclusively to initialize the shared event representation before task-specific optimization.Four downstream datasets are used and are divided by data provenance. CMS Open Data are used for the hypothesis-grid study (X → YHSM samples) and for anomaly detection using the 2016 DoubleMuon dataset45. The remaining studies use Delphes-simulated samples: dileptonic top-quark pair events for quantum-correlation measurements, and HSM → aa → 4b signal samples with ma = 30 GeV together with multijet backgrounds containing two or four b jets. All datasets are summarized in Extended Data Table 1.Data-splitting strategies are defined separately for each stage and downstream task to reflect their intended use and to avoid information leakage. For pretraining, simulated events are randomly split into training (70%) and validation (30%) subsets. No dedicated test set is used at this stage, as model evaluation is performed exclusively on downstream tasks. For the hypothesis-grid study, datasets are partitioned into two disjoint subsets: one used for training and validation and the other reserved for final evaluation. For anomaly detection, fivefold cross-validation is used to maximize statistical usage while maintaining strict separation between training and evaluation data in each fold. For the quantum-correlation and exotic Higgs studies, independent datasets are generated for training and testing, ensuring statistical orthogonality and eliminating overlap between training and evaluation samples.Model architectureThe transformer architecture provides a permutation-equivariant mechanism for modelling sets of physics objects through attention-based interactions65. To incorporate local geometric structure, we augment the transformer with k-nearest-neighbour message passing, yielding a hybrid point–edge transformer architecture26. The resulting point–edge transformer encoder serves as a shared backbone that maps reconstructed objects into a unified event-level representation, which is consumed by multiple task-specific heads (Fig. 1).Reconstructed physics objects, including jets, electrons and muons, together with their kinematic properties, flavour-tagging information, lepton identification and charge, are represented as particle clouds and provided as input to the backbone. During pretraining, a 10% feature dropout is applied by randomly masking input features on a per-sample basis to discourage over-reliance on specific features and to improve generalization to downstream tasks. The backbone supports both discriminative and generative objectives within a single representation space. Generative objectives are formulated using diffusion models66, which reconstruct clean inputs from progressively noised versions. The diffusion-time parameter t controls the noise level and defines a continuum between clean inputs (t = 0) and increasingly perturbed representations (t > 0). Discriminative and generative objectives are evaluated on representations sampled along this noise trajectory, enabling a consistent interface for both regimes within the shared backbone.The classification head predicts the physics process category of each event. During pretraining, the classification head predicts one of the ten physics-process categories listed in Extended Data Table 1: QCD, \(t\bar{t}\), \(t\overline{t}W\), \(t\overline{t}Z\), W + jets, Z + jets, WW, ZZ, WZ and HSM(WW*). Variations in decay channels within each process (for example, hadronic or leptonic decays) share the same process label. Classification is performed on representations sampled across diffusion-time steps, including both clean and noise-perturbed inputs. For downstream classification tasks, compatible layers of the pretrained classification head are retained, while the final class-dependent layers are replaced and randomly initialized to match the required output dimensionality. Unlike during pretraining, downstream classification is performed only on clean inputs.The classification loss is defined as \({{\mathcal{L}}}_{{\rm{class}}}={\alpha }^{2}(t)\,\,\text{CE}\,(y,{\hat{y}}_{{\rm{pred}}}),\) where \({\hat{x}}_{\mathrm{perturbed}}=\alpha (t)x+\sigma (t)\epsilon\), with limt→0α(t) = 1 and limt→1α(t) = 0, ϵ denoting Gaussian noise, \({\hat{y}}_{\mathrm{pred}}\) the prediction obtained from the noise-perturbed input and CE the cross-entropy. The factor α2(t) weights contributions at different perturbation levels.The assignment head predicts object-to-decay associations within a hierarchical representation consisting of resonances and their decay products. For each resonance r, an assignment tensor encodes the probabilities of mapping the n reconstructed particle-cloud objects to the dr decay products and has dimension \({n}^{{d}_{r}}\). Multiple transformer-based heads incorporating the symmetry tensor attention framework54,55 predict resonance reconstructability and assignment tensors while respecting permutation symmetries among identical decay products. Resonances sharing identical decay structures are processed by a shared head. Resonance attributes, such as masses, are provided as conditional inputs so the model can respect and exploit symmetries between resonances.The assignment loss follows the SPANet formulation54,55, combining a permutation-invariant cross-entropy loss for object assignments with a cross-entropy loss for resonance-reconstructability prediction. Non-reconstructable resonances are masked from the assignment term. The loss is reweighted to account for imbalances among reconstructability configurations.The segmentation head formulates resonance prediction as an object-detection problem following the DETR framework67 and its mask-based extensions68. A set of learnable queries is processed by a transformer decoder with cross-attention to the encoded particle-cloud representation and refinement via self-attention. Each query corresponds to a resonance candidate and is mapped to a class label and a segmentation mask over reconstructed objects.The segmentation loss follows the DETR-style set-prediction formulation67,68. During training, predictions are first associated with targets using Hungarian matching69, ensuring permutation invariance among resonance candidates. The matching cost includes classification and mask components. After matching, the loss combines a class-reweighted classification term with focal70 and dice71 mask terms, applied only to matched resonance targets.The unsupervised generative head defines a self-supervised pretraining objective based on diffusion-conditioned reconstruction. A masking module perturbs a subset of particle-cloud elements and provides a diffusion-time embedding that encodes the noise level for each perturbed point. The generative head conditions on the unperturbed portion of the event representation to reconstruct the perturbed inputs, corresponding to an inverse diffusion denoising task. Fully perturbing the particle cloud recovers the unconditional generation setting within the same formulation.The supervised generative head follows the same diffusion-based formulation as the self-supervised reconstruction objective but targets invisible event components. Inspired by the use of conditional diffusion models for neutrino momentum reconstruction in ref. 72, noised tokens representing invisible particles are injected into the particle cloud and reconstructed conditioned on the observed objects. The missing transverse momentum is included as a global event-level conditioning variable, allowing the model to learn the relationship between the event-wide transverse momentum imbalance and the invisible components. From the perspective of the shared backbone, supervised reconstruction of invisible components and self-supervised masked reconstruction correspond to the same diffusion-conditioned denoising operation, differing only in the choice of perturbed tokens. Task-specific decoders define the reconstruction targets in each case. Both objectives use the loss \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal L }}}_{\mathrm{generation}}=\parallel {\bf{v}}-{{\bf{v}}}_{\mathrm{pred}}{\parallel }_{2}^{2},\) where v and vpred denote the target and predicted diffusion vectors, respectively.Training procedure, software and hardwareModel training was performed on the Perlmutter supercomputer at National Energy Research Scientific Computing Centre (NERSC) using 512 NVIDIA A100 graphics processing units (GPUs) and 16,384 central processing unit cores. Only the self-supervised generative head was active, and the masking probability was increased progressively from 30% to 100% during training. In the second stage, all weights from the first stage were reused, and the network was trained jointly with the classification, supervised generative and self-supervised generative heads active.
